# R7 — Arrival in Jerusalem (19:28–48) + Temple Teaching (20:1–21:38)

**Range read in full:** raw 9441–9912 (slice complete)  
**Source:** Joel B. Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)  
**Sections:** §5.7 Arrival in Jerusalem; §6 Teaching in the Jerusalem Temple  
**Target slugs (when integrating):** [[luke]], [[joel-green]], [[jesus]], [[jubilee]]

## Claims

### C1 — Narrative bridge: journey ends; disciples recede; christology and division intensify
**Locus:** raw ~9441–9455 (slice ll. 2–7; intro to §5.7)  
**Quote:** "The journey to Jerusalem, begun in 9:51, comes at last to its finale… dual focus on Jesus’ identity and the division precipitated by his arrival in Jerusalem… gradual deemphasis on the disciples is matched… by a crescendoing preoccupation with christology… ‘the king who comes in the name of the Lord’ (v 38)."  
**Claim (Green):** 19:28–48 bridges disciple-formation on the way to temple instruction (20:1–21:38) and passion–exaltation (22–24). After 18:31–34 the twelve blur into “two of the disciples” / “whole multitude of the disciples”; Luke renews Davidic-messianic kingship (from 18:35–43; 19:11–27; birth narrative 1:32–35).

### C2 — Division in Israel reaches unprecedented strength at Jerusalem
**Locus:** slice ll. 5–7  
**Quote:** "Early on, Simeon had foretold that Jesus would be the cause of division within Israel (2:34–35)… The strength of the presentation of this motif in this narrative section is unprecedented… leaders looking for a way to execute Jesus (vv 47–48)."  
**Claim (Green):** Three division loci: praise vs. silencing demand (vv 37–40); city’s failure re peace and visitation (vv 42, 44); people spellbound vs. leadership seeking death (vv 47–48). Opposition height matches 6:11; 13:31 and fulfills passion predictions (9:22, 44; 17:25; 18:31–33).

### C3 — Jerusalem temple as “culture center”; destruction opens centrifugal mission
**Locus:** slice ll. 8–9  
**Quote:** "If Jerusalem is utterly destroyed (with no stone left on another, v 44), then its socio-religious role is also decimated… status distinctions it embodied and propagated are no longer definitive… citation of Isa 56:7 in v 46… sans the Isaianic phrase ‘for all peoples’… paves the way for a mission that is centrifugal rather than centripetal (cf. Acts 1:8)."  
**Claim (Green):** Citing Geertz-style “culture centers,” Green reads the temple architecture as ordering segregations (Jew/Samaritan/Gentile; male/female). City’s fall ends that world-ordering role; truncated Isa 56:7 refuses eschatological ingathering *to* Jerusalem and prepares Acts’ outward mission. Soteriology here is less explicit but present via the nature of the king’s dominion.

### C4 — Jerusalem as destiny and Holy City: confrontation with temple authority staged
**Locus:** slice ll. 28–29 (§5.7.1 intro)  
**Quote:** "Jerusalem has been vested with monumental significance. It is foremost the place of destiny… (e.g., 9:31, 51; 13:31–35; 18:31–34)… Holy City—location of the temple, abode of God, nexus between human and divine… How will Jesus… fare in relation to Jerusalem—the city, the temple, and its leadership…?"  
**Claim (Green):** Narrative time slows via Bethphage, Bethany, Mount of Olives. Regal messianic painting sets challenges to Jesus’ authority base and his demise (vv 39–40; cf. 20:2).

### C5 — Entry as Maccabean/Josephus-type royal entry: victory presupposed, not claimed
**Locus:** slice ll. 30–31  
**Quote:** "In analogous scenes, the person who enters the city does not do so in order to claim kingship; rather, entry presupposes an already achieved victory… Jesus is not about to assert his royal status… assumes the portrait of Jesus already established, with its soteriological emphasis on good news to those living on the margins… (4:18–19)."  
**Claim (Green):** Colt-to-acclamation sequence is eschatological/scriptural (Ps 118; Zech 9:9) certifying messiahship; kingship nature already developed (jubilee-echoing 4:18–19 good news to the marginalized). Secondary: Green cites Maccabean literature and Josephus for the type scene.

### C6 — Colt details carry royal parody (tied/untied; unridden; “The Lord needs it”)
**Locus:** slice ll. 35–38 (on 19:28–34)  
**Quote:** "the colt is tied and must be untied (mentioned five times!)—a possible echo of Gen 49:11… parody: The ruler of the Genesis text is characterized by extraordinary opulence, whereas the colt Jesus rides must be borrowed… ‘that has never been ridden’… Zech 9:9 LXX… ‘new colt’… claim of Jesus (as lord) supersedes the rights of ownership… (cf. 1 Sam 8:10–18)."  
**Claim (Green):** Particulars are royally laden yet fit Luke’s kingdom for the least and “nowhere to lay his head” (9:58). Prophetic omniscience, not prior arrangement: “found it just as he had told them.”

### C7 — Riding and cloaks: Zech 9:9 + Davidic coronation; disciples initiate messianic acclaim
**Locus:** slice ll. 40–41 (19:35–36)  
**Quote:** "That he now rides a colt, for only the last mile of the journey, intimates the symbolic character of this act… Zech 9:9… heirs of David rode to their coronation… in setting Jesus on the colt… they are taking their own initiative in acclaiming him as the Davidic Messiah… Jesus’ acquiescence… confirms that they are right to regard him as king."  
**Claim (Green):** Symbolic last-mile ride; disciples join Peter’s confession (9:20)—whether they grasp royal implications remains open.

### C8 — Ps 118 as royal-entry psalm; “the king” added; peace in heaven vs. on earth
**Locus:** slice ll. 42–52 (19:37–38)  
**Quote:** "Psalm 118… reverts to its earlier significance as a psalm of royal entry… addition of the words ‘the king’… origin in… Zech 9:9… ‘Peace in heaven’… In the former peace is said to be ‘on earth’ [2:14], while in the latter peace is ‘in heaven’… ‘Peace in heaven’… refers to the divine intention… full manifestation on earth interrupted by opposition to Jesus."  
**Claim (Green):** Not Tabernacles palm-festival focus (no palms). Disciples, not Jerusalem, fulfill 13:35’s conditional blessing—so connection is unhappy; city remains obdurate. Praise for “deeds of power” is theocentric: God works through Jesus as authorized agent of salvation.

### C9 — Final Pharisees: emblem of leadership resisting divine plan; stones would shout
**Locus:** slice ll. 54–60 (19:39–40)  
**Quote:** "last reference to Pharisees in the Third Gospel… exemplify all who set themselves over against the divine plan… ‘Teacher’… outside the circle of his followers… commencement of an historic clash of worldviews… messianic claims have been made on Jesus’ behalf. With his reply, Jesus embraces them… ‘stones’ would pick up the chorus…"  
**Claim (Green):** Request to silence betrays conviction that disciples oppose God’s will; Jesus affirms messianic acclaim and cosmic stakes of consummation. Tragic irony: city should welcome the king, not leave praise to stones.

### C10 — Weeping oracle: one charge—failure to recognize visitation and “things that make for peace”
**Locus:** slice ll. 62–76 (19:41–44)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ indictment against Jerusalem boils down to one charge: its failure to recognize God’s purposeful, salvific activity… (1) …‘on this day the things that make for peace’… (2) …‘the time of your visitation from God’… Peace… is a soteriological term—shalom… social, material, and spiritual realities… ‘now’ (v 42b)… point of no return."  
**Claim (Green):** Prophetic threat oracle (address / indictment / verdict) full of sorrow, not vindictiveness. Visitation hoped as salvation (1:68; 7:16) becomes judgment (cf. 10:8–15). “Things for peace” include the king and welcome/blessing responses. Pharisees of v 39 are proleptic of Jerusalem (and later joint rejection, 23:13–23).

### C11 — “Jerusalem” primarily cipher for temple system and leadership, not all Israel
**Locus:** slice ll. 76–77  
**Quote:** "Jerusalem’s ignorance and obduracy cannot be transferred to Israel as a whole or even… to all of Jerusalem’s inhabitants… ‘Jerusalem’ functions above all as a cipher for its role as a cultural center… temple system and the leadership… closed to the nature of the kingdom… prepares for… forgiveness (cf. 23:34; Acts 3:17; 13:27), but this possibility will not be realized in the case of those who continue to cling to the power structures supported by the temple ideology."  
**Claim (Green):** Temple holiness/purity segregation ideology self-legitimates resistance (cf. Acts 2–7). Sentence uses five military-destruction images and OT collage (Nebuchadnezzar/exile analogy): rejecting Jesus = covenant betrayal like that which led to first destruction.

### C12 — Temple entry is first adult temple visit; city ≈ temple; four-scene entry structure
**Locus:** slice ll. 90–92 (§5.7.3 intro)  
**Quote:** "first time Jesus has been in the temple since he was 12 years old… divine necessity of his being in his Father’s house… prefiguring his own teaching ministry… city of Jerusalem and the Jerusalem temple are virtually equated… move directly from a prophetic threat oracle against the city… to his dramatic, symbolic act of censure and recovery…"  
**Claim (Green):** Luke’s entry has four scenes (vv 28–48); acquisition + ride share royal-personage theme; temple act is terse yet heavily interpretive given buildup from 9:51.

### C13 — Cleansing reclaims temple for revelatory teaching; merchandisers “driven out” like demons
**Locus:** slice ll. 93–98 (19:45–46)  
**Quote:** "in his prophetic critique of the temple, Jesus recovers the temple for its legitimate use—namely, revelatory teaching concerning the purpose of God… ‘driving out’ objectionable people, in the same way that he ‘drove out’ demons… sacrificial system itself does not come under criticism… rationale… Isa 56:7 and Jer 7:11…"  
**Claim (Green):** Completes royal-entry type scene with cultic act (positive or negative). Outer Court of Gentiles; small-scale, highly symbolic. Mixed citation juxtaposes two construals of the temple.

### C14 — “House of prayer” = revelation + justice; “den of robbers” = leadership’s violent refuge
**Locus:** slice ll. 98–102  
**Quote:** "typically Lukan collocation of prayer and divine revelation in the temple… nature and present outworking of the divine plan… characterization of prayer in 18:1–8, 9–14 as the persistent pursuit of justice… ‘cave for bandits’… Jer 7:3–20… sanctuary for those who have committed… oppression of the poor… ‘robbers’ an apt… description of the Jewish leaders, whose economic power is grounded in… the temple."  
**Claim (Green):** Had the temple been truly a house of prayer, Jerusalem might have recognized visitation and peace. Citation stops short of “for all people”: temple as used demarcates insiders/outsiders; ironically universal-mission revelation still comes *in* the temple (2:25–32; Acts 22:17–21), but Gentiles are reached centrifugally.

### C15 — Daily temple teaching; sanhedrin triad seeks death; people as buffer (jubilee-echoing good news)
**Locus:** slice ll. 104–108 (19:47–48)  
**Quote:** "temple becomes an important site for Jesus’ ministry of teaching… orient the temple around its true significance as a place of ‘good news for the poor.’… message is similar to that in 4:16–30… use of the Scriptures of Israel to announce the dawning of eschatological salvation… triumvirate—the chief priests, scribes, and the leaders… sanhedrin… seek his execution… support of the crowds frustrates their quest."  
**Claim (Green):** Division people vs. leadership fulfills Simeon (2:34–35). Teaching content largely off-stage later; Luke privileges hostility the good news engenders. **Jubilee link:** temple reclaim aims at 4:18–19 / good news to the poor as legitimate temple use.

### C16 — §6 frame: inclusio teaching–people–temple; leitmotif = legitimate authority
**Locus:** slice ll. 111–124 (§6 intro)  
**Quote:** "20:1 forms an inclusio with 21:37–38… Jesus’ teaching, the people as the recipients… temple setting… leitmotif… conflict surrounding the question, Who has legitimate authority?… high politics and high worship originate from the same impulse, the Jerusalem temple… Jesus cannot afford a laissez-faire attitude toward the temple…"  
**Claim (Green):** Structure: (1) conflicts 20:1–40; (2a) Son of David who is Lord 20:41–44; (2b) dislegitimation of oppressive leadership 20:45–21:4; (3) calamity as old order yields to new 21:5–38. People receive instruction and buffer Jesus from arrest.

### C17 — Authority challenge (20:1–8): good news vs. sanhedrin status; John as test of divine origin
**Locus:** slice ll. 132–152  
**Quote:** "Accosting Jesus before the people, they seek to portray him as an outsider… shame him publicly by casting doubt on his authority base… ‘To bring good news’… inbreaking kingdom… privilege to those occupying low positions… ‘Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin?’… if… John’s message originated with God, this would be tantamount to admitting that Jesus’ ministry was itself sanctioned by God."  
**Claim (Green):** Leaders’ authority from birthright, education, status, temple proximity; Jesus’ known from Sonship/Spirit (1:35; 3:21–22; 4:18–19) and royal entry. Their claimed ignorance echoes 19:44 indictment; attempt to shame backfires; Jesus refuses answer but has implied divine authorization.

### C18 — Vineyard parable (20:9–19): beloved son; tenants not vineyard destroyed; leadership transfer
**Locus:** slice ll. 154–203  
**Quote:** "In Isaiah 5, the owner… pronounces judgment on the vineyard, not on the tenants… This is not the case here… Destruction of Jerusalem… does not mark the annihilation of Israel… consequences… their own devastation and the transfer of leadership to others, Jesus and his apostles… ‘my beloved son’… (3:22)… ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’… Ps 118:22; Isa 8:14–15; Dan 2:34–35, 44–45."  
**Claim (Green):** Spoken to the people, aimed at leadership (v 19). Slaves = prophets (incl. rejected John); tenants = Jerusalem leaders denying owner’s claim. Fruitfulness (since 3:7–9), not birthright/training/temple role, qualifies God’s people. Stone-complex: divine necessity of son’s death, exaltation prelude, judgment on violent tenants, warning to people. Leaders want to arrest but fear the people.

### C19 — Caesar tribute (20:20–26): trap between Rome and people; priority of temple at stake
**Locus:** slice ll. 205–218  
**Quote:** "question about the legality… of paying tribute to the emperor is also a question about the authority of the sanhedrin to serve as Rome’s agent… Much more, it is a question about Jesus’ fidelity to the temple… Will he go so far as to call into question the priority of the temple itself?… Jesus in a vice between Pilate and the people."  
**Claim (Green):** Continuity from vineyard episode; covert agents “pretending to be righteous” = self-justification by status, not modern hypocrisy. Tribute’s symbolic weight: economic burden, foreign subjugation (echo census 2:1–7), sedition risk (later 23:2), sanhedrin as collectors. Secondary/historical: annual denarius; 6 C.E. theocratic resistance to tribute.

### C20 — “Give back to Caesar… and to God”: prior claim of God, not two equal spheres
**Locus:** slice ll. 228–236  
**Quote:** "requesting from them a denarius… exposes… they, who possess denarii, also possess their own answer… ‘Give to Caesar what is his already’… not… dividing the world into two spheres… prior and more fundamental claim of God on all human beings… (16:13)… Jerusalem leadership appears to have sided with the Empire, against the purpose and rule of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Intertextual base Gen 1:26 (image) + law “inscribed” on persons. Empire/Wealth only within God’s dominion; when claims conflict, choose which dominion to serve. Trap’s Yes/No logic (king forbids tribute / allows and is no king) fails; wonderment and silence, not repentance.

### C21 — Sadducees/resurrection (20:27–40): battle over who interprets Moses faithfully
**Locus:** slice ll. 238–250, 289–298  
**Quote:** "real issue… nature of Jesus’ authority… scriptural faithfulness, and then authority to interpret Scripture faithfully… Scriptures are not for Jesus self-interpreting, but must be read from the right perspective… eschatological one… Who interprets Moses… faithfully?"  
**Claim (Green):** Artificial levirate riddle pits posterity-immortality (Torah) against resurrection. Jesus: two ages—this age marries; those worthy of that age / resurrection neither marry nor die, like angels, children of God. Middle-voice marriage language reorients patriarchal levirate objectification; hearing good news relativizes family (cf. 8:1–3, 19–20). Exod 3:6, 15: God of living patriarchs; “to him all of them are alive.” Scribes approve resurrection answer yet remain outsiders—will fail on Messiah and values (20:41–21:4).

### C22 — Messiah’s authority (20:41–44): “Lord” outranks “Son of David” as ultimate category
**Locus:** slice ll. 299–318  
**Quote:** "‘Son of David’ must not be the ‘ultimate category’ for understanding the identity of the Messiah… better category… is ‘Lord’ (cf. 2:11)… Only in… Acts… Pentecost address of Peter (esp. Acts 2:34–36)… exaltation to the right hand of God and installation as ‘Lord’ come via his resurrection and ascension…"  
**Claim (Green):** Ps 110:1 riddle against scribes’ interpretive authority even when they agree on resurrection. Lukan birth narrative still affirms Davidic messiahship; puzzle is relational ranking (father honors “my Lord”). “Enemies” footstool resonant in ch. 20’s hostility.

### C23 — Scribes’ despotic authority (20:45–47): status display + devouring widows
**Locus:** slice ll. 320–367  
**Quote:** "ultimate charge… participation in behaviors and… a system that victimizes widows… ‘Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes… best seats… places of honor… They devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.’"  
**Claim (Green):** Spoken to disciples in hearing of all the people—undermines leaders publicly and warns disciples (cf. 12:1; 22:24). Clothes/greetings/seats = nonverbal status claims (// 11:43; 14:7–11). Seeking abundance of honor yields abundance of condemnation. Faithful interpretation and faithful response are bundled.

### C24 — Widow’s gift (21:1–4): not exemplary piety but temple system that devours the poor
**Locus:** slice ll. 368–376  
**Quote:** "in no way does Luke suggest that Jesus finds the widow’s action exemplary or praiseworthy… religious system was supposed to care for such as these (cf. Acts 6:1–6), not render them utterly destitute… system, the temple treasury itself… feeds off those who cannot fend for themselves… inherent claim to divine legitimation… highlights the necessity of Jesus’ criticism of the temple… already begun in 19:41–48."  
**Claim (Green):** Analogy: scribes // wealthy donors; widows of 20:47 // this widow. Two lepta = her entire means of support vs. gifts from abundance. Mission is good news to the poor (4:16–30), not further impoverishment—**jubilee/poor-release trajectory** pressed against temple economy.

### C25 — Eschatological discourse setup: temple stones down; temple fall ≠ immediate End
**Locus:** slice ll. 377–401 (§6.2 intro; 21:5–7)  
**Quote:** "Jesus speaks of both [temple destruction and the End], but not in a way that marks the fall of the temple as the onset of the consummation… fall of Jerusalem as an eschatological event, but not in immediate relation to the coming of the eschaton… temporal priority of the fall of Jerusalem and… necessity of delay… yet maintains an emphasis on the imminence of the eschaton."  
**Claim (Green):** Structure: summary 8–11; then persecution/witness 12–19; fall + times of Gentiles 20–24; cosmic signs + Son of Man 25–28; readiness 29–36; narrative close 37–38. Herod’s aggrandized temple’s magnificence makes total annihilation stunning. Questioners: disciples/people line blurred (“Teacher” odd for disciples).

### C26 — Prospective summary (21:8–11): resist false messiahs and terror; calamities within divine purpose
**Locus:** slice ll. 422–429  
**Quote:** "explicit denial that the end time would come immediately after the fall of Jerusalem (v 9b)—effectively driving a temporal and, thus, hermeneutical, wedge between these two events… Do not go after them… do not be terrified… phenomena… are actually embraced within the divine purpose."  
**Claim (Green):** Secondary historical note: 60s C.E. messianic revolutionary recruitment. Criteria for genuine “in my name”: Jesus-like comportment, persecution, repentance/forgiveness message—not timing speculation (// Acts 1:6–7).

### C27 — Persecution first (21:12–19): opportunity to testify; Spirit/wisdom; endurance gains lives
**Locus:** slice ll. 430–440  
**Quote:** "‘Before all this occurs’… persecution… among Jews as well as among Gentiles… opportunity to testify… ‘I will give you words and a wisdom’… ‘not a hair of your head will perish’… guarantee that nothing happens apart from divine purview… ‘By your endurance you will gain your lives.’"  
**Claim (Green):** Proleptic of Jesus’ passion and Acts arrests/witness (narrative unity of Luke-Acts; Jesus trustworthy prophet; adversity inside divine plan; model for faithful witness). Hair-proverb ≠ absolute physical safety beside v 16’s deaths. Endurance = active hopeful fruit-bearing (8:15), not passive waiting.

### C28 — Jerusalem surrounded (21:20–24): days of vengeance; exile collage; dual “times of the Gentiles”
**Locus:** slice ll. 441–449  
**Quote:** "omen… ‘When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies’… ‘days of vengeance, as a fulfillment of all that is written’… virtual collage of scriptural texts… fall… at the time of the Exile… ‘times of the Gentiles’… dual reference… Gentiles as God’s agents in… destruction and subsequent occupation… [and] proclamation of the good news among the Gentiles."  
**Claim (Green):** Narrative sequence after persecution implies causal judgment for resisting Jesus/followers (// 19:43–44; 20:9–18). No explicit restoration motif here; focus shifts (as Acts 1:6–8) from Israel-speculation to Gentile mission. OT “days of vengeance” could anticipate restoration, but co-text turns to Son of Man, not restored Jerusalem.

### C29 — Cosmic signs and Son of Man (21:25–28): theophany; redemption for the faithful
**Locus:** slice ll. 450–457  
**Quote:** "third stage… cosmic signs leading to the advent of the Son of Man… Dan 7:13… return of Jesus as a theophany… ‘your redemption is drawing near’… and ‘the kingdom of God is near’ (v 31)… ‘you’… those who are faithful… not to Jerusalem specifically."  
**Claim (Green):** Fall of Jerusalem and End are distinct phases; temporal gap unspecified beyond “not… immediately” (v 9). Nations fear; disciples stand with raised heads. Birth-narrative “redemption” of Israel/Jerusalem (1:68; 2:38) re-signified toward faithful responders.

### C30 — Fig tree and readiness (21:29–36): delay incorporated; “this generation” = resistant people
**Locus:** slice ll. 458–465  
**Quote:** "constant readiness and prayer are applicable… in all seasons preceding the eschaton… ‘this generation’… has regularly signified a category of people who are resistant to the purpose of God… less to say about the eschatological timetable and more… about the motif of conflict… old world, ‘this generation,’ does not easily give way to the new… ‘like a trap’… ubiquitous… alertness and prayer…"  
**Claim (Green):** Kingdom nearness includes present ministry *and* end consummation; whole sequence (persecution, fall, signs) points to fullness. Jesus’ words permanent like Yahweh’s word. Temptations of delay: dissipation, drunkenness, worries of this life (// 8:13–14; 12:45–46). Goal: strength to escape and “stand before the Son of Man.”

### C31 — Temple-teaching inclusio close (21:37–38): every day; people support; Mount of Olives custom
**Locus:** slice ll. 466–468  
**Quote:** "form an inclusio with 20:1, marking… closure… of Luke’s narration of the teaching of Jesus in the temple… ‘every day’… overwhelmingly positive response of ‘the people’ (‘all!’)… transition to… suffering and death… support… holds the hostile plans of his enemies at bay… departing each night to the Mount of Olives (→ 22:39)."  
**Claim (Green):** Exemplary “one day” (20:1) characterizes ongoing ministry. Festival lodging pressure explains nightly exit; Unleavened Bread/Passover timing only explicit at 22:1.

### C32 — Whole §6 arc: reclaim temple → rebuff → censure → destroy; authority and poor at center
**Locus:** slice ll. 397–398 (synthesis restated at §6.2)  
**Quote:** "Jesus had entered Jerusalem seeking to reclaim the temple for its proper use. His efforts at reform and message of the salvation of God on behalf of ‘the poor’ (cf. 4:18–19) have been rebuffed… censures those who refuse to hold themselves accountable to God (20:9–19) and use… the temple system to tyrannize… (20:45–21:4), and he now pronounces the destruction of the temple—indeed, the cosmic calamity soon to come as the old world gives way to the new (21:5–38)."  
**Claim (Green):** Master plot of 19:45–21:38: legitimate authority of Jesus (divine) vs. temple leadership (status/power); fate of temple/city as judgment when cultural center resists jubilee-shaped good news to the poor.
